newsitem.title: USA: U.S. EPA proposes imported gasoline rule changes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. EPA proposes imported gasoline rule changes.

text.p: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Wednesday proposed changes in policies on imported gasoline to let foreign refiners petition the agency to get similar treatment to U.S. refiners.

Under the proposal, which stemmed from a World Trade Organization decision, foreign refiners could petition the EPA to set an individual baseline reflecting the volume and quality of gasoline shipped to the United States in 1990.
The refiner then would have to meet the same requirements on using individual refinery baselines as domestic refiners.
The agency also proposed monitoring the quality of imported gasoline, so it could "adjust the standards" for imports if their quality was lower than the average baseline set for domestic refiners.

The agency also proposed other requirements for overseas refiners related to tracking movement of gasoline from the refinery to the U.S. border, and for monitoring compliance and enforcement actions to correct violations.

"EPA considers the proposed rulemaking would be consistent with the agency's commitment to fully protect the public health and the environment, and with the United States' commitment to ensure that the regulation is consistent with the obligations of the United States under the World Trade Organization," the EPA statement said.

The WTO in a decision last year sided with Venezuela and Brazil which complained that the EPA's previous rule discriminated against foreign refiners by holding them to a different standard than U.S. refiners.

While U.S. refiners were to be able to use their individual baselines of 1990 production to measure quality of their gasoline, foreign refiners were to use a national average of the baselines of U.S. refiners to measure compliance.
Venezuela and Brazil said that would hold them to a higher standard than the U.S. refiners that fell below that average.
